## Metabolic flux sensing of sugars in Saccharomyces cerevisiae

Abstract

A canonical view of nutrient sensing is that cells sense the concentration of nutrients. However,

it is sometimes beneficial to regulate cellular processes based on the metabolic flux through a pathway,

instead of the concentration of a nutrient. The mechanisms to achieve metabolic flux sensing remain

largely unclear. The observation of flux-dependent regulation is also limited.

This dissertation work explores the phenomena and mechanisms of metabolic flux sensing of sugars

in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Galactose and glucose are two types of sugar used by cells as

carbon sources for growth. Cells sense the sugars for proper regulation of their metabolism. In the case

of galactose, cells sense galactose for deciding the induction of the galactose-utilization (GAL) pathway.

In the case of glucose, cells sense glucose for repressing genes involved in utilizing other carbon sources.

To study the metabolic sensing processes, first, a series of tools are developed to enable the necessary

genetic perturbation and control of metabolism in living cells. A high-throughput imaging method is

developed to monitor the perturbations and measure signaling readout of the pathway. Then, we study

the signaling role of galactokinase Gal1 in the GAL pathway, and report that the enzyme can couple its

catalytic activity to signaling, resulting in a signaling output proportional to the metabolic flux. Next,

in the glucose repression pathway, I find that glucose repression depends on metabolic flux of glucose.

However, I rule out the signaling role of hexokinase Hxk2, and find that Mig1 controls glucose repres-

sion via a non-canonical mechanism. Some candidate metabolites potentially for determining glucose

repression are identified through differential perturbations of glycolytic metabolites and model predic-

tions. Last, I describe a growth curve measurement device I developed, which enables easy and accurate

measurement of growth curves.

## Introduction

## Nutrient sensing in Saccharomyces cerevisiae

Budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a rather ubiquitous distribution, ranging from human-

associated environments for food and beverage, to natural environments on the surface of fruits, tree

bark, rotten wood, and in the soil of primeval forest [1–3].

Yeast cells can utilize a variety of nutrients in the environment. They can use various sugars, in-

cluding glucose, fructose, mannose, galactose, sucrose, maltose and raffinose, as well as non-sugar

sources, including glycerol, ethanol and acetate, as the sole carbon source. They can also use a variety

of nitrogen-containing compounds, including various amino acids and ammonium, as the sole nitro-

gen source. From the provided nutrients, they can synthesize all amino acids and various vitamins for

their growth.

Yeast cells also handle a wide range of nutrient concentrations. They utilize sugars efficiently from

molar to millimolar level. In the alcoholic fermentation of grape juice, the initial concentration of glu-

cose and fructose is usually 16–26% (w/v) total, and can be as high as 50% (w/v) [4]. S. cerevisiae cells

maintain high fitness in such an environment of juice fermentation, overtaking other microbes and

dominating population in the mid and final stage [5].

1


<!-- Page 14 -->


Because of its importance in fermentation, it is not surprising that there is a long history studying

the metabolism of yeast. This leads to the revealing the metabolic pathway of alcoholic fermentation

[6], and the discovery of enzyme regulation [7] in the first half of the 20th century.

One key question in yeast metabolism research is how cells sense the nutrients available and ad-

just their metabolism and growth. Substantial progress has been made in understanding the nutrient

sensing pathways and the signaling networks. The response to many nutrients have been extensively

studied [8, 9]. For example, the GAL pathway for utilizing galactose, the glucose repression pathway

for repressing the expression of other enzymes when glucose is available, Snf1/AMPK pathway for sens-

ing the energy status of a cell, HOG (High Osmolarity Glycerol) MAPK pathway for responding to

high osmolarity environments, PHO pathway for responding to phosphate level, GCN pathway for

internal amino acid sensing, TORC1 pathway for responding to nitrogen sources, cAMP/PKA (cyclic

AMP/Protein Kinase A) pathway for central regulation of metabolism and growth, Ras/cAMP path-

way for coupling glucose signals to cAMP.

Many of these pathways have counterparts in mammalian cells with same or different functions,

and they play important roles in homeostasis, development and diseases.

## Metabolic flux sensing of sugars

A canonical view of nutrient sensing is that cells sense the concentrations of nutrients, either extracellu-

larly or intracellularly. However, sensing the concentration of a nutrient has its limitations, because it is

sometimes beneficial to regulate cellular processes based on the metabolic flux through a pathway.

Some evidence of flux sensing has been reported. In E. coli, it is found that the metabolic flux

through glycolysis is sensed by sensing the concentration of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (FBP), and the

concentration of FBP is proportional to the flux through glycolysis [10–12]. In budding yeast S. cere-

visiae, the Ras/cAMP/PKA pathway is found to respond to FBP, allowing glycolytic flux to be coupled

to the activation of PKA [13], although it does not strictly confirm a flux-based mechanism or show a

flux-dependent regulation.

I attempt to identify flux-dependent regulation phenomena, and illustrate the flux-sensing mecha-

2


<!-- Page 15 -->


nisms in this dissertation work.

In the GAL pathway, we notice that the galactokinase Gal1 is more than an enzyme, which catal-

yses the phosphorylation of galactose. Gal1 not only has an enzymatic function, but also a signaling

function. Gal1 can bind the downstream signaling protein Gal80 in the GAL pathway, in the presence

of galactose and ATP. We hypothesize that this would couple the enzymatic reaction to signaling, allow-

ing Gal1 to sense the flux through the reaction. Using metabolic enzymes as sensors is an elegant bio-

logical design. Understanding the properties of the flux-sensing enzyme and its role in GAL pathway

signaling would help establish a new mechanism of flux sensing, which is distinct from the mechanism

which senses a flux-correlating metabolite.

In the glucose repression pathway, there are various observations of flux-dependent regulation.

Glucose repression was found to correlate with hexokinase activity in 1989 [14]. The correlation be-

tween hexokinase expression level and glucose repression is also observed in another context in recent

years [15]. However, it is not fully known what glucose repression responds to intracellular glucose

concentration or glucose flux. It is also unclear what mechanism may allow the sensing of glucose flux.

Interestingly, an enzyme — hexokinase Hxk2 is frequently indicated to be the glucose flux sensor [16].

Some complex mechanisms have been proposed for Hxk2 to have signaling function, involving changes

in Hxk2 phosphorylation state, localization and its complex formation with Mig1 [17–19]. But the ev-

idence of such a mechanism is still limited [20]. We attempt to find out whether glucose repression is

flux-dependent and what the mechanism of the flux sensing is. The hypothesis of Hxk2 being the po-

tential flux sensor is quite appealing. Exploring such a hypothesis can expand our understanding of flux

sensing enzymes.

Studying metabolic sensing in vivo involves engineering the necessary genetic changes to perturb

the metabolic sensors, the metabolic flux, monitoring the signaling output, as well as understanding

and eliminating native regulations which can complicate results. New tools are needed to address the

technical challenges in the research of metabolic sensing.

## Overview of the dissertation

In Chapter 1 of this dissertation, I introduce multiple technologies to handle the challenges of engineer-

ing the metabolic pathways and making measurements. The tools developed in this chapter are critical

for the work in later chapters of this thesis.

In Chapter 2, we explore the signaling role of galactokinase and the hypothesis of galactokinase be-

ing a fluxing sensor in the GAL pathway. We find that the signaling role of galactokinase helps stabilize

the galactose pathway regulation.

In Chapter 3, flux sensing in the glucose repression pathway is studied. We find that glucose repres-

sion indeed depends on glucose metabolic flux instead of glucose concentration. We exclude the roles

of all previously characterized glucose sensors in this process. The long-standing hypothesis of hexoki-

nase being the primary flux sensor for glucose repression is also ruled out. Finally, we find that control

of glucose repression by metabolic flux involves non-canonical regulation of Mig1 activity.

In Chapter 4, we attempt to identify metabolites which determine glucose repression without

knowing the sensor. Various metabolic perturbations are designed to differentially modulate metabo-

lites. Fluorescent biosensors are used to monitor the metabolic changes, and a glycolysis model is used

to predict other metabolites. By observing the correlation between metabolites and glucose repression

in various perturbations, we narrow down the number of metabolites potentially determining glucose

repression.

In Chapter 5, an electronic device is developed to greatly simplify growth curve measurement. It

monitors the optical density of microbial cultures when the cells are growing in culture tubes. The

device gives high-quality growth curves and makes it possible to perform growth curve measurements

on a routine basis.

## 1

## Developing tools for studying metabolic

## sensing in vivo

Studying metabolic sensing often involves perturbing metabolic or signaling pathways while observ-

ing changes in signaling or other cell states. However, it is often challenging and time-consuming to

construct the desired strain with complex genetic perturbations. In this chapter, I introduce multiple

technologies to handle the challenges, making it practical to implement the experiments in the last sec-

tion of this chapter, and in later chapters of this thesis.

### 1.1 Expansion of MoClo Yeast Toolkit

### 1.1.1 CRISPR-enhanced genome editing for building strains with complex

## genotype

Deleting genes and integrating expression cassettes are common tasks when constructing strains for

studying metabolic signaling.

The complexity of typical tasks can be demonstrated with the example of the glucose repression

pathway. If we need to modulate hexokinase level and observe glucose repression signaling with a fluo-

rescent reporter. Introducing the fluorescent reporter involves the integration of an expression cassette.

Because glucose is primarily phosphorylated by two hexokinases (Hxk1 and Hxk2). Modulating hex-

okinase level involves deletion of two major hexokinases and expressing one of the hexokinases under

inducible expression. Therefore, the task involves deletion of two genes and insertion of two expression

cassettes, a total of four edits. More genome editing would be needed if attempts are made to alter the

signaling pathway.

The high efficiency of homologous recombination and low rate of non-homologous end join-

ing make it relatively easy to perform genetic modification in S. cerevisiae. A series of shuttle vectors

(e.g. the pRS series [1, 2]), gene disruption cassette plasmids (e.g. pFA series [3]), and convenient yeast

strains (e.g. BY4741/BY4742 [4] and more BY series strains [2]) have been developed in the 1980s and

1990s for efficient genetic modification.

However, it is often advantageous to use prototrophic strains when studying metabolic signaling.

It is reported that perturbations in histidine, leucine, methionine and uracil biosynthesis can affect the

expression of up to 85% of genes in the genome, and the transcripts with more than twofold changes

are enriched for metabolic activity [5]. Repairing the auxotrophies after genomic engineering can be a

solution, but the amount of work is impractical in experiments involving many strains.

Avoiding auxotrophic markers means fewer options of selection markers. Therefore, it is essential

to make it possible to re-use markers.

8


<!-- Page 21 -->


Marker recycling with the Cre-LoxP system allows repeated use of the same marker [6]. This makes

it possible to perform complex genomic editing, e.g. the knock-out of 20 transporter genes [7], without

being limited by the number of markers available. However, marker recycling with Cre-LoxP is not

only time consuming, because it doubles the number of genomic editing steps. The recombination of

LoxP scars can even result in undesired gene losses and chromosomal rearrangement [8].

CRISPR/Cas9 generates targeted double-strand breaks, increases the rate of donor DNA homol-

ogous recombination at the target site. This makes it possible to eliminate the use of selection marker

in the DNA integrated [9]. Multiple works demonstrate such ability of marker-free genome editing

without integrating selective markers into the genomes [10–12]. Toolkit has also been developed [13].

Shaw et al. describes a set of versatile CRISPR tools in a blog post in 2018 [14] allowing efficient

workflow of genome editing. The tools are developed with the Yeast MoClo Toolkit (MoClo-YTK)

[15], combining with an improved sgRNA expression structure [10], and the gap repair assembly of co-

transformed Cas9 and sgRNA expression fragments in yeast [11]. This strategy allows to have the Cas9

and yeast selection marker on one plasmid, and sgRNA on a separate plasmid without yeast selection

marker. Therefore, it is not necessary to pre-determine the yeast selection marker when cloning sgRNA

plasmids, or to clone the same sgRNA into multiple plasmids with different markers. The choice of

selection marker and sgRNA combination can be determined at the time of yeast transformation. Iter-

ative editing can be performed by using Cas9 plasmid with a different marker in the next editing step.

The previous Cas9 plasmid will be lost spontaneously soon after selection pressure is removed.

moter pRPL18B), and various yeast selection markers, including three auxotrophic markers URA3,

LEU2, HIS3, and four antibiotic markers KanR, NatR, HygR, ZeoR.

Three antibiotic markers (KanR, NatR and HygR) are tested in yeast transformation experiments

in this work. Auxotrophic markers are not used in order to minimize metabolic perturbations from the

### 1.1.1.2 Selection of integration sites

When auxotrophic markers are used, new expression cassettes are often integrated to the loci of the

marker genes. Alternative integration sites need to be identified and tested, when we don’t use aux-

otrophic markers.

One popular integration site is the HO locus. HO is a non-essential gene encoding an endonuclease

involved in mating type switching. The gene and its regulation are well studied.

One way to integrate to HO locus inserts the new expression cassette between two genes without

disrupting the HO coding sequence. However, it can be difficult to determine the proper position for

insertion. For example, MoClo-YTK integrates 1262 bp before the HO CDS and swaps out a 52 bp

non-coding region (-1314 to -1263). However, HO has a long promoter with elements extending nearly

2 kb, with the URS1 region between -1900 and -1000 [19]. Therefore, the insertion changes the regula-

tion of HO, and the integrated cassette can also be affected by the regulation from the URS1 of HO.

Another way to integrate to HO locus involves swapping out the promoter and most of the coding

sequence of HO. This removes the native gene regulation at this locus, and minimizes the effects to

downstream genes by keeping changes far away from downstream gene. Although this strategy disrupts

the HO gene, because the function of the disrupted gene is well studied, the effect of its knock-out is

predictable.

Alternative integration sites used in literature include the dubious ORF YBR032W [20–22]. How-

ever, YBR032W is located closely upstream of EDS1, which is a paralog of glucose-responsive transcrip-

tion factor RGT1. Therefore, it is not the best option to perturb this locus when studying metabolic

signaling.

A series of new integration sites are proposed in [13, 23], and in a more recent work [24]. The pro-

posed integration sites are located in intergenic regions. However, the determination of the intergenic

regions is simply based on the distance to the upstream and downstream gene. However, yeast promot-

ers can be longer than 1 kb [25], also as shown in the HO example above, being 1 kb away from the

downstream gene still may not be truly intergenic, and can still be within the promoter regions of the

downstream gene.

11


<!-- Page 24 -->


Identifying conserved motifs in intergenic regions [26] can be helpful in identifying conserved regu-

latory elements and avoid disrupting regulation of the downstream gene.

An alternative approach to workaround the issues is to use well-studied non-essential genes as in-

tegration sites. Such genes can be safely disrupted, because they are responsible for other well-known

cellular processes. The popular HO locus is an example of such a gene.

Genes including AGA1 and AGA2 are identified based on such criteria. AGA1 and AGA2 genes

encode well-studied cell wall-associated agglutinin proteins involved in agglutination during mating.

Because this work does not depend on the mating pathway, they are good candidates to serve as integra-

tion sites. Transcript isoform profiling data [27] are examined to identify the transcribed regions of the

upstream and downstream genes. Alignment of DNA sequences of five species S. cerevisiae (Scer), S.

bayanus (Sbay), S. kudriavzevii (Skud), S. mikatae (Smik) and S. paradoxus (Spar) is performed as pro-

posed in [26] to identify conserved regulatory elements. The upstream boundaries of the integration

sites are selected to be after the mRNA 5’-end of upstream gene, and before the conserved elements in

the promoters of AGA1 and AGA2. The downstream boundaries of the integration sites are selected

within the CDS of AGA1 and AGA2 and away from their terminators, downstream promoters, and

downstream transcribed regions.

To validate the new integration sites, a weak pCYC1-mVenus construct and a strong pTDH3-

mVenus constructs are integrated to each of the selected sites with CRISPR-enhanced integration. As

expected, no growth defect is observed. Then, YFP level of the strains is measured with flow cytometry.

The expression of all constructs is comparable when integrated to HO, AGA1 and AGA2 sites. There-

fore, these three integration sites are later used throughout this work. Having three integration sites is

sufficient for this work, attempts are not made to identify more integration sites.

### 1.1.1.3 Gene deletion donor DNA design for iterative editing

When performing gene deletion with CRISPR, Cas9 generates a double-strand break targeted by

sgRNA, and a donor DNA is used as template for cells to repair the double-strand break via homoge-

nous recombination. This replaces the deleted region with the sequence of the donor DNA, eliminat-

12


<!-- Page 25 -->


ing the sgRNA target site and preventing it from additional cuts from Cas9.

After deleting the gene, it is sometimes necessary to insert back the wild-type gene or a mutant in

a later experiment. Such iterative editing of the locus after deletion requires the presence of a sequence

which can be targeted by sgRNA. And it is necessary to design the donor DNA used in the gene dele-

tion step to make it targetable.

Therefore, donor DNA is designed to replace the deleted gene with a short 20-bp barcode. The bar-

code always contains a PAM sequence to allow subsequent sgRNA-targeting. The design process is au-

tomated with a Python script. First, a series of 20-bp random barcode sequences with 18-bp random se-

quences ending with GG are generated. primer3 [28] is used to screen for barcodes with around 60 ◦C

Tm and free from secondary structures or homodimer formation. Then the barcode is concatenated

with upstream and downstream sequence homologous to the target gene to delete. Secondary struc-

tures are checked again, so that adding the homology sequence does not make it more prone to hair-

pin or homodimer formation. Finally, on-target score of the sgRNA protospacer to target the barcode

is predicted with Azimuth model [29], which runs in a local Docker container and exposes a HTTP

based API, because this open-source model depends on specific versions of Python packages. On-target

score of more than 0.7 is aimed. Results are written in a Genbank file with the oligo sequences, and the

sequence and annotations of the locus after the gene deletion. This allows easy importing and visualiza-

tion in other softwares.

Short 40-bp homology arms are usually enough for targeting a locus in yeast. However, increasing

the length of one homology arm to 60 bp is observed to improve gene deletion efficiency, and increas-

ing the other arm to 60 bp does not further improve efficiency. Therefore, homology lengths of 40bp

on one side and 60bp on the other side are used for most gene deletions and PCR targeted integration.

I propose a split selection marker design, in which the coding sequence of yeast selection marker

marker, and the split KanR marker. The split KanR marker plasmid is linearized with EcoRV before

yeast transformation. After gap repair in yeast, the linearized plasmid will be identical to the circular

plasmid with normal KanR marker.

In a yeast transformation, the linearized split-marker plasmid shows 10 times transformation effi-

ciency compared to the circular plasmid with normal KanR marker. Such efficiency improvement can

be critical in applications where high efficiency is needed, for example transforming a large library. It

### 1.1.1.5 Single-fragment gap-repair Cas9-sgRNA plasmid

The two-fragment CRISPR tools in [14] allows flexible selection of selection marker and sgRNA tar-

gets, because one fragment contains Cas9 with a selection marker, the other fragment contains sgRNA

for the target.

However, such flexibility is not always necessary. Certain loci are targeted more often, for example

the HO, AGA1 and AGA2 integration sites. Additionally, the approach is less reliable when delivering

multiple sgRNAs for targeting multiple sites. Because there is no selection for the entering of all differ-

ent sgRNA variants.

To address the issue, it will be good to have a single-fragment version of Cas9 plasmid with sgRNA

on the same plasmids. The finding in the section 1.1.1.4 allows me to do that without sacrificing the

transformation efficiency gain from transforming the linearized fragment of a plasmid. I designed the

Cas9 plasmid to use the split-marker design to transform it as a linearized fragment and re-circularizing

via gap repair after entering cells. To allow flexibility of assembling one or more plasmid, the plasmid

is designed to be use with the golden gate cloning approach. sgRNA can be PCRed from the two-

fragment design after the sgRNA is validated with a few standard primers, and integrated to the one-

fragment design in one step.

This also generates a series of plasmids targeting the common loci including HO, AGA1 and AGA2

with different antibiotic selection markers. The main advantageous to use the one-fragment design

in this case is that it saves a gel extraction step when preparing the Cas9 plasmid for transformation,

simplifying the workflow.

### 1.1.4 Localization tags

Nuclear localization signal. Regulation of nuclear-cytoplasmic localization is a common phenome-

non of multiple proteins of interest in this work, for example Mig1 [36] and Hxk2 [37]. Identifying the

nuclear region of cells is helpful when studying the nuclear-cytoplasmic localization. The localization

of the proteins can be highly dynamic [38], prompting the need for live-cell imaging in some exper-

19


<!-- Page 32 -->


iments. Targeting fluorescent proteins to nuclei with localization tags is a very helpful tool allowing

simple live-cell imaging.

Nuclear localization signal (NLS) is widely used to tag proteins for nuclear import in yeast and

other organisms. Fluorescent proteins can be tagged with NLS for visualizing the nuclei. A series of

NLS variants have been studied in yeast [39–41], including the classical monopartite NLS motif (ES

PKKKRKVE) of simian virus 40 (SV40).

However, using such NLS can involve more than just adding it to any protein. To improve nuclear

localization, concatenation of multiple NLS is often used, and adding the tags to different localization

of a protein can also affect nuclear targeting [42].

Bipartite NLS tag has been shown to have higher binding affinity to importin and improved lo-

calization in vivo [39, 40]. For example, the artificial bipartite SV40 NLS (KRTADGSEFESPKKKRK

VE)[39]. This is consistent with the fact that importin structure shows two NLS-binding pockets on

the surface [43]. To avoid NLS-tagged proteins from affecting NLS-importin binding, linker sequences

are added before and after the NLS following a previous work which studies their binding affinity [39].

Both SV40 and bipartite SV40 (BPSV40) NLS shows efficient nuclear targeting efficiency, when

fused to mTagBFP2 and imaged with fluorescence microscopy. BPSV40 NLS is used for all later experi-

ments in this work.

Plasma membrane tag. Having accurate ground truth of the cell boundary is critical for training

neural network models for cell segmentation. However, even for human experts, it can be hard to de-

termine the precise boundary of a yeast cell in bright-field microscopy. Plasma membrane tagged flu-

orescent protein can help marking the true boundary of cells and providing the ground truth for cell

segmentation.

Fusing fluorescent proteins to a plasma membrane localized proteins, e.g. plasma membrane trans-

porters, can target the fluorescent protein to the plasma membrane. However, when fluorescent pro-

tein is fused to Gal2 or Hxt transporter, localization is not limited to plasma membrane, but also in the

vacuole. Such localization further depends on growth conditions and is regulated by signaling [44].

Tagging endogenous genes with fluorescent protein is useful for studying the expression level and local-

### 1.2 Highly customizable framework for automation of micros-

## copy systems

### 1.2.1 Introduction

The work described in this thesis heavily relies on fluorescent protein-based measurement. Fluorescent

proteins can be fused after promoters for understanding the transcriptional regulation of genes. They

can also be fused to the coding sequencing of proteins to monitor the expression level and localization

of the proteins. Additionally, genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors enable the measurement of

certain metabolites in living cells. Fluorescent biosensors for measuring protein kinase activity are also

becoming available.

In fluorescent protein-based measurement with microscopy, measurement at single cell level is

straightforward, and repeated measurement of the same cell over time is also not complicated. Further,

because minimal sample preparation is needed, it is easy to scale up the measurements for handling

many samples. This is especially important when we need to study the response of cells with different

genotypes in many different conditions.

Compared to flow cytometry, microscopy offers higher sensitivity, especially in the case of red flu-

orescent proteins, where most photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) start to have greatly reduced quantum

efficiency. Although microscopy has lower throughput in terms of the number of cells analyzed per

second, the higher measurement sensitivity and lower measurement uncertainty can often compensate

for the disadvantage, because less cells are needed to reach the same or better data quality of quantifi-

cation. In our experiences, both reduced number of cells needed in measurements and the faster speed

switching between samples, makes microscopy faster than flow cytometry, especially in our experiments

involving one or more 96-well plates of samples.

Quantifying fluorescence of cells in multi-well plates format is not a common application of micros-

copy, especially when we need to use high-NA oil-immersion objective for better signal quality, when

29


<!-- Page 42 -->


we need to search focus when focus is lost after moving across a well-plate, when we often have different

sample layouts in different experiments, and when different fluorescent channels and exposure time

are needed for different wells. Many microscopy softwares simply do not have the flexibility to perform

those tasks.

Open source microscope control software μManager [63, 64] is widely used for controlling micro-

scopes for custom applications. It offers the flexibility through scripting capability and programming

interface for implementing custom image acquisition routines. Additionally, Micro-Magellan [65] and

Pycro-Manager [66] build on top of μManager to provide higher level functionalities to simplify image

acquisition of biological samples.

However, despite being able to achieve our image acquisition tasks, most image acquisition and

visualization software lacks the native support for sample management. This means there is no easy

way to quickly go through the images of each position of a well-plate for quality control or quick image

analysis by eyes in the middle of an experiment. Although μManager offers great flexibility, we find

that additional speed-up of image acquisition is possible when controlling the camera and filter wheels

with low-level manufacturer API to optimize the sequence of actions and to parallelize some actions.

The reduction of image acquisition time is critical, if we need to finish imaging half a 384-well plate

on the timescale of 1 hour, to avoid additional signaling changes inside the cells in longer experiments.

Additionally, because the μManager based ecosystem has a complex architecture, it can be challenging

to set up due to compatibility issues, for example related to Java-based μManager/ImageJ UI and the

Python-Java bridge of Pycro-Manager.

More broadly, custom microscope hardware or applications often face challenges in device con-

trol and image acquisition automation. The issue is more significant in advanced microscope systems,

e.g. in the case of stimulated Raman microscopy [67–69], which involves non-standard hardwares, in-

cluding tunable laser systems, and sometimes optical spectrometers, optical power meters, electronic

test-and-measurement devices, etc. Although it is possible to write custom μManager Device Adapters

and treat them as ’Generic Device’ type, the efforts and complexity to implement that outweigh the ad-

30


<!-- Page 43 -->


vantage, especially before the release of μManager 2.0 and its moving away from the legacy Windows

XP and Visual Studio 2010 for Device Adapters compilation during development.

Additionally, a microscopy system may additional involve microfluidics-based sample handlings

[70], online image analysis and event-driven acquisition [71], and more.

However, despite the advances in microscopy methods, image analysis and visualization tools, the

development of image acquisition software is quite limited. In a review article from 2012 [72], μMan-

ager and ScanImage [73] are the only two image acquisition software listed. Ten years later, the land-

scape basically remains unchanged, while the perspective article about bioimaging software usability

from 2012 is also still very relevant [74].

In the case of image visualization and analysis tools, new generation tools such as Napari [75] have

emerged with a vibrant ecosystem. The Python-based program is easier to integrate with Python-based

image analysis ecosystem and modern machine learning libraries for neural-network-based image analy-

sis, replacing the widely-used ImageJ [76, 77] and Fiji [78] in many applications.

A new generation of image acquisition framework is also needed for improved usability, for the

flexibility to control non-standard hardwares and microfluidics systems, for easier integration with im-

age analysis for online image analysis and event-driven acquisition, without sacrificing the support for

legacy microscopy hardwares. Such advancement in image acquisition framework would allow people

with less software engineering and hardware control expertise to benefit from microscopy automation,

reduce human efforts and mistakes during experiments, and perform tasks impossible with manual

controls.

In this section, I briefly describe a highly customizable framework for the automation of micros-

copy systems. Software for controlling the microscope in our lab is built on top of the framework.

Early versions of the software have been used in previous publications from the lab [79, 80]. Experi-

ences and feedback from early experiments have been incorporated in the current design.

This framework should be considered as experimental, and further work is still needed for complet-

ing the framework for a broad range of users. Although only features necessary for image acquisition

experiments in this thesis are currently implemented, more types of devices and applications are kept in

mind during the design of the framework.

### 1.2.2 Key design considerations of the software framework

Device abstraction and programming interface. Most devices can be abstracted as property–

value pairs, with the exception of data-heavy tasks of getting imaging data from a camera. Therefore,

devices are abstracted as having a series of property nodes. The hierarchy of nodes is not allowed, be-

cause it is rarely necessary. To allow representing layers of nodes for human-readability, character / is

allowed in the name of a device property.

Devices in the main program are “connected” to an abstract device hub to allow enumeration. Pro-

gramming interface allows remote reading and modifying the properties via gRPC interface.

A remote device can also be “connected” to the device hub through a gRPC interface. The con-

cept of remote device would allow implementing the control of a device with another programming

language, such as Python, by users.

User interface. User interface is a crucial feature of the software. Showing the status of all devices is

critical for troubleshooting issues. Visualizing images in a way optimized for the image acquisition can

make it easier to adjust settings before an experiment, and also make it possible to monitor the experi-

ment for issues, such as the loss of focus, air bubbles in immersion oil, etc.

In this software, device status is shown in a clear way in the right panel, different channels of an

image are intentionally shown separately, separate image contrast adjustments for different channels are

placed next to the image channel. These image acquisition-targeted designs are quite unique compared

to other open-source microscopy softwares built on top of the image visualization tools.

To make it easier to navigate in a 384-well plate, a unique feature of the user interface is the plate

map in the left panel, which shows the current position based on the XY-coordinate obtained from the

XY-stage. This simple feature greatly improves the efficiency and reduces human errors when working

with 384-well plates of samples.

TIFF format in a ZIP file. ZIP file has a central directory near the end of the file, which would allow

users to get the list the name of all files in the ZIP file. Having a single ZIP file also makes it more ef-

ficient to copy the image data to a remote server or simply moving to a larger mechanical hard drive.

allows using the image name without really overwriting the previous image. This prevents accidental

overwrite of files in experiments, which is not rare in practice. In Python, images in the ZIP file can be

accessed with zipfile library without unzipping the file.

Z-Standard (zstd) compression is used to compress the image data inside the TIFF file, instead of

using the compression mechanism of ZIP. Although zstd compression limits the compatibility of the

TIFF file, and makes it incompatible with ImageJ, the almost 50% decrease in file size outweighs the

ImageJ incompatibility issue. The files can be opened conveniently with tifffile library in Python.

The Python-based Napari can be used for visualization as an alternative to ImageJ.

Image acquisition tasks. Multi-channel acquisition of a field of view is controlled by the main pro-

gram implemented in C++. This makes it possible to perform low-level optimization of the sequence

of commands issued to different devices and handle the device status changes with the multithreading.

However, to allow sufficient flexibility, the control logic to move to a specified position and perform

the multi-channel acquisition is implemented in the Python library. The Python library additional im-

plement the pre-acquisition and post-acquisition logic, such as checking the number of cells already

acquired to determine whether to move to the next well, initial image segmentation after acquiring an

image, and search for focus if the perfect-focus system fails after moving a long distance across a multi-

well plate.

Image analysis tasks. The software can include some image analysis capabilities, but the complex

image analysis steps should be handled with external modules via gRPC. For example, the program

uses the U-Net model for cell segmentation. The U-Net model is served with TensorFlow Serving run-

ning in a Docker container on the same computer. The preprocessing, postprocessing, and quantifica-

tion are done by the main software. This both ensures efficiency and consistency of the image analysis

pipeline, and also maintains the stability of the main program. After a graphics card driver change, the

Docker container may fail until a restart, but other functions of the main program are not affected.

### 1.3 Understanding glucose repression in the GAL pathway

Results in this section contribute to the paper: Chiara Ricci-Tam, Ishay Ben-Zion, Jue Wang,

Julius Palme, Ang Li, Yonatan Savir & Michael Springer. Decoupling transcription factor

expression and activity enables dimmer switch gene regulation. Science 372, 292–295. doi:

10.1126/science.aba7582 (2021).

The galactose-utilization (GAL) pathway in budding yeast S. cerevisiae has been extensively studied

as a model system for metabolic sensing and signal integration.

The presence of galactose promotes the transcriptional activation of GAL genes, while glucose,

the preferred carbon source, inhibits the GAL gene expression. When both galactose and glucose are

present, the GAL genes respond to the ratio of galactose and glucose. More specifically, The fraction

of cells which activate the GAL pathway depends on the ratio of galactose and glucose concentration

in the medium [81]. However, when most cells are activated, the expression level of GAL1 gene in the

induced fraction solely depends on glucose concatenation in the medium [79].

Understanding the determining factor of GAL1 expression is especially important when GAL1

expression level is used as the readout of GAL pathway activation, as is the case with Chapter 2 of this

thesis when we study the metabolic flux sensing of galactose. Therefore, we need to look at how glucose

and galactose signals are integrated to control GAL1 expression.

mVenus. The plasmid construction is simplified with a standard reporter backbone plasmid I devel-

research and the conserved elements identified by alignmenting of DNA sequences of five species S.

## Abstract

Nutrient sensors allow cells to adapt their metabolisms to match nutrient availability by

regulating metabolic pathway expression. Many such sensors are cytosolic receptors that

measure intracellular nutrient concentrations. One might expect that inducing the metabolic

pathway that degrades a nutrient would reduce intracellular nutrient levels, destabilizing

induction. However, in the galactose-responsive (GAL) pathway of Saccharomyces cere-

visiae, we find that induction is stabilized by flux sensing. Previously proposed mechanisms

for flux sensing postulate the existence of metabolites whose concentrations correlate with

flux. The GAL pathway flux sensor uses a different principle: the galactokinase Gal1p both

performs the first step in GAL metabolism and reports on flux by signalling to the GAL

repressor, Gal80p. Both Gal1p catalysis and Gal1p signalling depend on the concentration of

the Gal1p–GAL complex and are therefore directly correlated. Given the simplicity of this

mechanism, flux sensing is probably a general feature throughout metabolic regulation.

### 2.1 Introduction

Nutrient sensing systems allow cells to adjust metabolism to their environment by sensing changes in

extracellular conditions. There are two main known types of sensors: plasma membrane receptors [1]

and cytosolic receptors [2, 3]. Plasma membrane receptors measure extracellular conditions directly by

sensing extracellular nutrient concentrations. Cytosolic receptors measure intracellular nutrient con-

centrations, which are affected by both extracellular conditions (supply) and intracellular metabolism

(demand). Thus, nutrient sensing systems that rely on the intracellular nutrient concentration cannot

distinguish whether receptor sensing changes because of changes in supply or demand: the intracellu-

lar nutrient concentration could decrease because of a decrease in supply, for example, when a nutrient

is no longer available in the environment, or because of an increase in demand, for example, when en-

zymes of a metabolic pathway are produced. This ambiguity could be problematic because changes in

supply and changes in demand probably require different cellular responses. Nevertheless, many nutri-

ent sensing systems rely on intracellular nutrient concentrations, raising the question of whether there

45


<!-- Page 58 -->


are additional mechanisms that disambiguate these measurements.

Different regulatory mechanisms have been proposed that would solve this problem by unambigu-

ously correlating intracellular nutrient concentrations with physiologically relevant quantities. One

proposed mechanism results in the correlation of the intracellular nutrient concentration with extracel-

lular nutrient concentrations [4]. This was achieved in mathematical models by matching any change

in the expression of catabolic enzyme genes (demand) with corresponding changes in the expression

of transport genes (supply). Coordinating the expression of these genes prevents changes in intracellu-

lar nutrient concentrations. Therefore, the intracellular nutrient concentration is only responsive to

changes in supply, for example, in the extracellular nutrient concentration. However, the implementa-

tion of this mechanism in cells is complicated by the need to finely balance the production and activity

of the proteins responsible for supply and demand across physiological and evolutionary timescales.

An alternative proposed mechanism results in the correlation of the intracellular nutrient concen-

tration with demand, that is, metabolic flux. Flux sensing would be a useful biological property, and

there has been some phenomenological evidence that flux sensing occurs in multiple metabolic path-

ways [5, 6] and transporters[7–9]. While no mechanism has been found by which flux can be directly

measured, flux can be inferred by sensing the concentration of metabolites that are correlated with

flux [10–12]. The initial model that achieved a correlation between nutrient concentration and flux re-

quired a complex interplay of allosteric and transcriptional regulation of the metabolic pathway [12]. A

recent model proposed a simple mechanism for achieving the correlation but required thermodynamic

constraints in the corresponding biochemical reaction [13]. Currently, few biological instantiations

where such correlations are used to regulate nutrient sensing have been described.

The mechanisms that correlate intracellular nutrient concentrations with metabolic flux or extracel-

lular conditions have mostly been described theoretically; the contribution of these mechanisms to nu-

trient sensing in cells is unclear. In this study, we combined theory and experiments to investigate the

effect of changing supply and demand on the galactose-responsive (GAL) pathway of Saccharomyces

cerevisiae. We find that the GAL pathway contains a flux sensor. This flux sensing is not achieved by

correlating intracellular nutrient concentrations with metabolic flux, but by a new mechanism that

46


<!-- Page 59 -->


measures metabolic flux at the level of a metabolic enzyme.

### 2.2 Results

### 2.2.1 Signalling in the GAL pathway increases with increasing flux.

To illustrate how substrate metabolism affects sensing of intracellular substrate concentrations, we first

constructed a toy model in which substrate molecules were transported into a cell through a trans-

porter, and then either activated a concentration sensor or were metabolized by an enzyme (Fig. 2.1a,

Supplementary Note 1 in Section S2.3.1 and Extended Data Fig. S2.1). As expected, in this simple

model increasing metabolic enzyme levels led to a decrease in signalling (Fig. 2.1b).

We compared this prediction to the behavior of the GAL pathway of S. cerevisiae (Fig. 2.1c), a well-

studied model system for nutrient sensing [14, 15]. In this pathway, the concentration sensor Gal3p sig-

nals after binding to intracellular galactose, leading to the expression of enzymes involved in galactose

metabolism [16–18]. One of these enzymes is Gal1p, a galactokinase that catalyses the first step of GAL

metabolism. Throughout the article, we refer to this signalling process that results in GAL1 expression

as ‘GAL signalling’.

To investigate how galactose metabolism affects GAL signalling, we varied the level of fluorescently

tagged Gal1p by placing the expression of a GAL1 -mScarlet-I fusion gene under the control of an in-

ducible promoter, and measured GAL signalling in this strain by placing mVenus expression under the

control of the GAL1 promoter. Surprisingly, increasing the Gal1p level increased GAL signalling (Fig.

2.1d, P < 0.0001).

We hypothesized that this unexpected result could be due to signalling by Gal1p itself. Like Gal3p,

Gal1p can regulate GAL signalling: both the Gal3–galactose complex [17, 19–21] and the Gal1p–galac-

tose complex [19, 22–24] bind the GAL repressor Gal80p, thus upregulating GAL gene expression.

The role of Gal1p in GAL signalling has often been ignored as the basal expression of GAL1 is too low

to activate GAL signalling on its own [15, 25, 26] and most studies of the GAL pathway have focused

on the activation of GAL signalling. However, once the GAL pathway is upregulated, the amount

To understand why sensing the flux through Gal1p could be useful, it is important to understand

how this flux relates to the overall flux of galactose through metabolism. Because galactose metabolism

is a single, unbranched pathway (Extended Data Fig. S2.1a), the steady-state flux through every reaction

is equal. Therefore, sensing the flux through Gal1p is sufficient to measure the metabolic flux through

the pathway. In addition, Gal1p flux is equal to the net transport (or uptake) flux of extracellular galac-

tose. This is true because any galactose molecule that is imported and not lost by being exported will be

metabolized by Gal1p. As all these fluxes are equivalent, we refer to them as ‘galactose flux’ throughout

the article.

Based on the mechanism we propose, flux sensing should be a unique behavior of Gal1p; the canon-

ical galactose sensor Gal3p should not be a flux sensor. In contrast to Gal1p, the Gal3p–galactose com-

tional to. Therefore, we propose that Gal3p acts as a classical galactose concentration sensor (Fig. 2.2b)

and only Gal1p acts as a galactose flux sensor.

To identify potential experimental perturbations that clearly distinguish if Gal1p or Gal3p sense the

galactose flux or the galactose concentration, we first analyzed the two types of sensors in the toy model.

A simple perturbation could be to vary the extracellular substrate concentration, and thus change flux.

As flux and flux sensor signalling must be correlated, this perturbation should equally change flux and

flux sensor signalling. However, varying the extracellular substrate concentration could also change the

intracellular substrate concentration, and therefore concentration sensor signalling. Therefore, this per-

would be to vary the sensor protein level. Varying the level of the sensor protein can affect both sig-

nalling and flux for a flux sensor (Fig. 2.2a), but only signalling for a concentration sensor (Fig. 2.2b).

The experimental difference between the two behaviors can be magnified by simultaneously changing

both the extracellular substrate concentration and the level of the sensor protein. For a flux sensor, vary-

ing the sensor level and the extracellular substrate concentration leads to all measurements of flux and

signalling to lie on the same line (Fig. 2.2c). In contrast, for a concentration sensor, varying the sen-

sor level and the extracellular substrate concentration leads to measurements of flux and signalling to

lie on different lines for each sensor level (Fig. 2.2d). In summary, the relationship between flux and

signalling does not depend on the sensor level for a flux sensor but depends on the sensor level for a

concentration sensor.

To test this prediction experimentally, we constructed strains in which we could vary Gal1p or

Gal3p levels while varying the extracellular galactose concentration. We deleted both endogenous ga-

lactose sensor genes (GAL1 and GAL3) and introduced either GAL1 or GAL3 under the control of an

inducible promoter. As the inducible GAL3 strain would not be able to metabolize galactose because

of the absence of GAL1, we constitutively expressed a signalling-deficient galactokinase gene (SpGAL1).

To ensure that flux measurements would not be influenced by signalling feedback, we also expressed

the genes for GAL80 (GAL regulation), GAL2 (galactose import), and GAL7 and GAL10 (galactose

metabolism) from strong, constitutive promoters (Methods).

First, we measured the relationship between galactose flux and GAL signalling at different Gal1p

levels. Consistent with the flux sensor prediction (Fig. 2.2c), varying the Gal1p level did not change

the relationship between galactose flux and GAL signalling (Fig. 2.2e). Next, we measured the relation-

with the concentration sensor prediction (Fig. 2.2d), the relationship between galactose flux and GAL

signalling depends on the Gal3p level (Fig. 2.2f).

It is worth noting that galactose flux and GAL signalling are only correlated until a plateau in sig-

### 2.2.3 Gal1p flux sensing has a unique signalling regime.

Next, we analyzed the modelling data from Fig. 2.2 to determine how increasing sensor levels affects

signalling instead of how it affects the relationship between flux and signalling. We found that flux and

concentration sensors behaved identically at low sensor levels: increasing the sensor level increases sig-

nalling (Fig. 2.3a,b, regime I). Surprisingly, flux and concentration sensors behaved differently at high

sensor levels (Fig. 2.3a,b). Concentration sensor signalling saturated at the signalling limit (Fig. 2.3b,

regime III), while flux sensor signalling saturated below the signalling limit (Fig. 2.3a, regime II). In this

regime, the flux sensor displayed a unique behavior where signalling is independent of the sensor level,

but still responsive to changes in the extracellular substrate concentration (2.3a, regime II).

The independence of signalling and the sensor level is caused by the catalytic activity of the flux sen-

sor. For a concentration sensor, that is, a sensor protein with no catalytic activity, increasing the sensor

level increases the concentration of sensor proteins that can bind the substrate and thereby the concen-

tration of the sensor–substrate complex. Therefore, increasing the sensor level increases signalling (Fig.

2.3b, regime I). For a flux sensor, increasing the sensor levels has a second, opposing effect. Because

of the catalytic activity of the flux sensor, increasing the flux sensor level also decreases the intracellu-

lar concentration of substrate molecules that can bind flux sensor proteins. When the two opposing

effects of increasing the flux sensor level are perfectly balanced, the concentration of the flux sensor–

substrate complex remains constant. In this situation, increasing the flux sensor level would not in-

crease signalling.

Regime II, where signalling is independent of the flux sensor, corresponds to a limit in the trans-

pathway flux is controlled by substrate transport (Extended Data Fig. S2.3a). This also means that the

substrate transport reaction is maximal for the given transporter level and extracellular substrate con-

centration (Extended Data Fig. S2.3c). Because this maximal transport flux determines pathway flux

in the flux limit, it also determines flux sensor signalling (Supplementary Note 4 in Section S2.3.4 and

Extended Data Fig. S2.3d). Notably, this design allows flux sensor signalling to be independent of the

sensor level but responsive to changes in the extracellular galactose concentration (Fig. 2.3a, regime II).

Thus, flux sensor signalling can measure the extracellular environment in a way that is robust to any

changes in flux sensor level arising from gene regulation or gene expression noise.

The model creates experimentally testable predictions for the galactose sensors Gal1p and Gal3p.

Specifically, the model predicts that increasing the level of the flux sensor Gal1p or the concentration

sensor Gal3p should increase GAL signalling until reaching different limits, the flux limit or the sig-

nalling limit. These limits can be distinguished because only the flux limit depends on the maximal

transport flux and therefore on the extracellular substrate concentration (Fig. 2.3a,b). In addition, as

described in Fig. 2.2, the signalling limit can be determined genetically by deleting the GAL80 gene

(Fig. 2.3c,d, regime III); this orthogonal measurement can be compared to the limits that are observed

when increasing sensor levels.

To test which limits are reached by Gal1p and Gal3p, we experimentally varied their levels by in-

creasing their expression from an inducible promoter. We found excellent agreement between the flux

sensor predictions and the Gal1p data (Fig. 2.3a,c), and the concentration sensor predictions and the

Gal3p data (Fig. 2.3b,d). Increasing the Gal1p level increases GAL signalling when the Gal1p level is

low (Fig. 2.3c, regime I), but reaches the flux limit when the Gal1p level is high (Fig. 2.3c, regime II).

As predicted, signalling in the flux limit is responsive to changes in the maximal transport flux: chang-

ing the extracellular galactose concentration (Fig. 2.3c, regime II) or the level of the transporter Gal2p

the flux limit, Gal1p titration does not reach the signalling limit (Fig. 2.3c). In contrast to Gal1p, in-

creasing the Gal3p level continuously increases GAL signalling (Fig. 2.3d, regime I) until reaching

the signalling limit where signalling is no longer responsive to the extracellular galactose concentra-

tion (Fig. 2.3d, regime III). Together, these experiments confirm that flux sensing by Gal1p enables a

unique regime, the flux limit, where GAL signalling is independent of Gal1p level but responsive to the

extracellular galactose concentration.

The flux limit is reached by endogenous GAL regulation. In our experiments, we controlled the

Gal1p level by expressing GAL1 from an inducible promoter; this resulted in Gal1p levels that were

high enough to reach the flux limit (Fig. 2.3c, regime II). In WT cells, GAL signalling controls the

Gal1p level, raising the question whether this endogenous regulation allows Gal1p levels that reach

found that in the absence of galactose, the Gal1p level is too low to reach the flux regime (Extended

we describe above, increasing the level of a metabolic enzyme like Gal1p can decrease the intracellular

concentration of its substrate. Initially, this might not be a problem because the enzyme level is low

and only leads to a negligible decrease in the intracellular substrate concentration (Extended Data Fig.

S2.3b, regime I) as the enzyme has a high flux control coefficient (Extended Data Fig. S2.3a). However,

eventually increasing the enzyme level will transfer flux control to a different reaction (Extended Data

signalling is only regulated by Gal3p concentration sensing, we observed that increasing the SpGal1p

level only had small effects on GAL signalling when the SpGal1p level was low, but strongly reduced

GAL signalling once the SpGal1p was high (Fig. 2.1h). In contrast, when GAL signalling is regulated by

Gal1p flux sensing, increasing the Gal1p level increases GAL signalling at low Gal1p levels (Figs. 2.1d

and 2.3a, regime I). Moreover, at high Gal1p levels, Gal1p flux sensing has the useful property that

GAL signalling is constant regardless of fluctuations in Gal1p level, but responsive to changes in the

extracellular galactose concentration (Fig. 2.3a, regime II). Therefore, we hypothesized that the physio-

logical role of Gal1p flux sensing is to compensate for the decrease in Gal3p concentration sensing that

occurs when galactose flux increases, thereby ensuring the stability of GAL signalling, that is, the ability

to maintain GAL signalling at a given signalling level as long as the extracellular galactose concentration

is constant.

If the physiological role of Gal1p flux sensing is to compensate for decreasing Gal3p concentration

sensing, Gal1p flux sensing should not be needed when there is no galactose flux. We removed galactose

flux and Gal1p flux sensing by deleting the GAL1 gene. To determine whether GAL signalling is stable

after deleting GAL1, we used time-lapse microscopy to identify cells with high levels of GAL signalling

after 10 h of growth in a medium with galactose (see Extended Data Fig. S2.8 for the population dis-

tributions of GAL signalling). We then monitored GAL signalling in these cells for the following 4 h.

The reporter for GAL signalling we used in previous experiments, the expression of mVenus from the

GAL1 promoter, is not suitable for these experiments because the fluorescent protein is stable over this

time span. Therefore, we replaced mVenus with an actively degraded fluorescent protein fusion, that

is, mNeonGreen-Ubi-Y. Surprisingly, we found that while GAL signalling is stable in the WT strain,

it is unstable when GAL1 is deleted (Figs. S2.8a and S2.9a). This indicates that Gal1p flux sensing is

required for stable GAL signalling even in the absence of galactose flux.

We reasoned that GAL signalling is unstable when GAL1 is deleted because of transcriptional feed-

back by the GAL repressor GAL80. Gal3p signalling leads to the expression of GAL80. Gal80p in turn

potential to destabilize GAL signalling. When GAL1 is present, this negative feedback could be com-

pensation would not occur, resulting in unstable GAL signalling. To test this hypothesis, we removed

this negative feedback by replacing the GAL80 promoter with a constitutive promoter. Indeed, in this

constitutive GAL80 expression background, GAL signalling is stable even when GAL1 is deleted (Figs.

Using strains with constitutive GAL80 expression removes the confounding effect of negative

this stability requires Gal1p flux sensing, we removed Gal1p flux sensing, but not galactose flux, by re-

placing the GAL1 coding sequence (CDS) with the SpGAL1 CDS, which has no signalling activity in S.

cerevisiae (Extended Data Fig. S2.2b). Replacing only the CDS maintains the ability of GAL signalling

to increase galactose flux by increasing the galactokinase level. In this strain, GAL signalling is unstable

We note that this instability occurs in the presence of positive feedback through increased GAL2 expres-

not destabilize signalling (Figs. S2.8c and S2.9c). These results indicate that positive feedback through

GAL2 is neither necessary nor sufficient for stable GAL signalling. Similarly, we found that abolish-

ing Gal3p concentration sensing by deleting GAL3 does not destabilize GAL signalling (Fig. 2.4c, P

= 0.28). These results indicate that the stabilization of GAL signalling is a physiological role that is

unique to Gal1p flux sensing.

### 2.3 Discussion

In this study, we showed that Gal1p is a flux sensor. We argue that this flux sensing arises from the bi-

functional nature of Gal1p. Since both Gal1p activities, catalysis and signalling, depend on the forma-

59


<!-- Page 72 -->


tion of the Gal1p–galactose complex, they are inherently coupled: the signalling activity of Gal1p is

always proportional to the catalytic activity of Gal1p. Because of this coupling, Gal1p effectively senses

galactose flux.

Gal1p flux sensing acts in parallel with the canonical galactose sensor Gal3p, raising the question

of why two different galactose sensors regulate GAL signalling. A possible explanation is that having

two sensor genes allows for two distinct transcriptional profiles [15, 25, 26, 32]: in the absence of galac-

tose, GAL3 is expressed while GAL1 is not. In turn, in the presence of galactose, GAL1 is expressed at

substantially higher levels than GAL3. These distinct transcriptional profiles define two distinct phys-

iological tasks for the two sensors. As described before, basal GAL3 expression enables Gal3p concen-

tration sensing to activate GAL signalling when galactose is first encountered [30, 31]. As we described

in this study, the increase in GAL1 expression in the presence of galactose enables Gal1p flux sensing to

stabilize GAL signalling when galactose is metabolized (Figs. 2.1 and 2.4). The transcriptional profiles

thus divide the general task of regulating GAL signalling into the two specialized tasks of activating and

stabilizing GAL signalling.

In addition to having distinct tasks, Gal1p and Gal3p also sense distinct properties; specifically,

Gal3p activates GAL signalling based on the intracellular galactose concentration and Gal1p stabilizes

GAL signalling based on the galactose flux (Figs. 2.2 and 2.3). We suspect that these properties help

Gal1p and Gal3p accomplish their respective specialized tasks. Consistent with this idea, the activation

task of Gal3p concentration sensing can only partially be accomplished by Gal1p flux sensing: when

the GAL3 CDS is replaced by the GAL1 CDS, growth in galactose is delayed [26, 33]. We do not have

direct data that Gal3p concentration sensing cannot replace Gal1p flux sensing solely for the sensing

function as we never created a strain where both GAL3 and a signalling-deficient galactokinase gene

have the transcriptional profile of GAL1. However, our data provide a hint as to why galactose sens-

ing in this strain could be problematic. Expression of GAL3 from the more inducible GAL1 promoter

would lead to high Gal3p levels in the presence of extracellular galactose. This could mean that Gal3p

signalling reaches the signalling limit where Gal3p signalling is no longer responsive to the extracellular

galactose concentration (Fig. 2.3d, regime III). This constitutive signalling would be a problem when

60


<!-- Page 73 -->


extracellular galactose decreases because it would lead to the superfluous expression of GAL genes. Elu-

cidating this interplay between the physiological roles of the two sensors and the properties they sense

will be the subject of future work.

Even though the mechanism of flux sensing we report in this study has not, to our knowledge, been

described before, we believe that it is ubiquitous. As we outline below, we reason that this is true be-

cause the mechanism is simple to evolve, leveraging features that are already common for metabolic

enzymes but difficult to detect with traditional experimental approaches.

The biophysical feature that underlies Gal1p flux sensing can be described as ‘reverse allostery’.

When galactose binds to the active site of Gal1p, the surface conformation of Gal1p changes [18, 24],

allowing binding to Gal80p. This constitutes a flow of information from the active site to distal surface

sites. Allostery, a common and widely appreciated form of metabolic regulation, is the inverse of this

process: the flow of information from distal surface sites to the active site. As energy is not used in this

process, from a thermodynamic perspective, information must simultaneously flow in both directions.

Indeed, recent work showed that sites of allosteric regulation can be predicted by measuring reverse al-

lostery, that is, identifying how substrate binding at the active site leads to conformational changes at

distal surface sites [34–36]. If allostery is a common feature of metabolic enzymes and the flow of infor-

mation is bidirectional, reverse allostery must be equally common. This indicates that many metabolic

enzymes meet the biophysical requirements for flux sensing.

To achieve flux sensing, reverse allostery must regulate a secondary activity of the metabolic enzyme.

Minimally, this requires that the metabolic enzyme carries out a secondary activity in addition to its

canonical catalytic activity. Such secondary activities, often described as ‘moonlighting’ activities, are

now being reported for many metabolic enzymes [37–40]. Thus, metabolic enzymes are increasingly

appreciated as multifunctional proteins, suggesting that the presence of a secondary activity—a prereq-

uisite for flux sensing through reverse allostery—is also a common feature of metabolic enzymes.

If flux sensing through reverse allostery is a common mechanism, why has it not been found pre-

viously? In the context of metabolism, such mechanisms are easy to miss. Typically, metabolic regula-

tion has been studied by deleting individual genes. This approach is often not possible for metabolic

61


<!-- Page 74 -->


enzymes because of essentiality: 75% of the essential genes of S. cerevisiae are involved in metabolic

processes [41]. Even for metabolic genes where deletions are viable, the effects of the deletion are diffi-

cult to disentangle. Gene deletions perturb both metabolic flux through the enzyme and any potential

signalling activity of the enzyme. This makes it difficult to distinguish whether the deletion changes

metabolic regulation because of indirect effects (caused by the perturbed metabolic flux) or direct ef-

fects (caused by the perturbed signalling activity).

If regulation by reverse allostery is indeed common, this mechanism could couple metabolic flux

to a wide range of cellular processes. Reverse allostery is flexible and not limited to regulating bind-

ing to other proteins. Existing examples of moonlighting activities include regulation at other control

points by binding to DNA and RNA [42, 43]. In addition, reverse allostery is not limited to regulat-

ing binding. For proteins with multiple catalytic activities, reverse allostery could lead to regulation

of one catalytic activity based on another catalytic activity. Such a design would allow one metabolic

flux to directly regulate another metabolic flux. More generally, reverse allostery or ‘catalysis-induced

enzyme movement’ has been proposed to perform work in cells, that is, ‘stirring’ the cytosol [44, 45].

Beyond the naturally occurring regulation through reverse allostery, we envision that advances in de

novo protein design will allow synthetic biologists to design proteins that specifically recognize the

substrate-bound state of the enzyme and thereby couple metabolic flux to any arbitrary cellular process.

In conclusion, this study provides a framework for the identification, characterization and de-

sign of flux-sensing systems in metabolic pathways. We anticipate that applying this framework more

broadly will establish flux sensing as a general theme of metabolic regulation. The mechanism of reg-

ulation by reverse allostery has implications beyond flux sensing: in principle, this mechanism should

be able to report the activity of any arbitrary enzyme that displays conformational changes during its

catalytic cycle.

### 2.4 Methods

### 2.4.1 Strain construction

All strains were derived from FY4. Yeast transformations were performed using a standard lithium ac-

etate protocol [48]. For chromosome integration, a selectable Cas9 expression plasmid was cotrans-

formed with a single-guide RNA expression cassette targeting the chromosomal site, and homologous

donor DNA to repair the double-strand break [49]. Plasmids for yeast transformations were cloned

using Gibson assembly and the yeast MoClo toolkit [50] (see Supplementary Table S2.1 for a list of

strains, Supplementary Table S2.2 for a list of plasmids and Supplementary Table S2.3 for a list of

oligonucleotides).

Fluorescent reporters for GAL1 expression. The GAL1 promoter sequence was amplified from

genomic DNA using PCR and cloned in front of a codon-optimized mVenus CDS followed by the

ADH1 terminator. For a reporter with decreased half-life, the GAL1 promoter was cloned in front of

the mNeonGreen CDS fused to ubiquitin-N-degron [51] with a glycine-serine linker followed by the

GAL1 terminator.

Gene deletion. For gene deletion, the region from the start codon up to the stop codon was replaced

with unique 20-bp sequences. Annealed oligonucleotides with 40–60 bp homology sequences to both

the gene promoter and the stop codon-terminator were cotransformed for homologous recombination.

Gene titration. PCR-amplified CDS sequences were cloned as fusion proteins with a C-terminal

yeast codon-optimized mScarlet-I tag, linked by a glycine-aspartate-glycine-alanine-glycine-serine and

followed by the TDH1 terminator. Expression of the cloned CDS was controlled by a synthetic pro-

moter consisting of seven tet operator sites followed by a CYC1 minimal promoter. The plasmid also

contained the transcription factor rtTA2s-M2 CDS flanked by the MYO2 promoter and the ADH1

terminator.

### 2.4.2 Culture conditions

Strains were grown in synthetic minimal medium consisting of 1.7 g L−1 yeast nitrogen base, 5 g L−1

ammonium sulphate and variable concentrations of galactose, glucose and raffinose. For the titration

experiments, the medium was supplemented with seven DOX concentrations, ranging from 2 µg mL−1

to 0.01 µg mL−1 in 2.44× dilution steps or no DOX. For the microscopy experiments, a low-fluores-

cence yeast nitrogen base lacking folic acid and riboflavin was used. Cultures were grown in 1.3-mL

96-well plates in a humified incubator at 30 ◦C with orbital shaking at 999 rpm.

### 2.4.3 Steady-state GAL signalling measurements

Strains were streaked out from −80 ◦C glycerol stocks on yeast extract peptone dextrose plates. Colo-

nies were picked into 1 mL yeast extract peptone dextrose and incubated for 24 h. Cultures were then

used to inoculate a cell dilution series in 500 µL 2% raffinose medium (supplemented with DOX when

appropriate). After 16 h, the optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of cultures was measured using a Syn-

ergy H1 plate reader (BioTek). Cultures with OD600 values between 0.025 and 0.075 were washed

twice using centrifugation (3000 g, 3 min) and resuspension in synthetic minimal medium without

any carbon sources. A 5-μl washed culture was used to inoculate 500 µL of medium containing galac-

tose, glucose and, when appropriate, DOX to an inoculation OD600 of 0.0005. After 8 h, cultures were

washed three times using centrifugation (3000 g, 3 min) and resuspension in Tris-EDTA buffer (10

mM, 1 mM EDTA). Washed cells were analyzed using an S1000EX flow cytometer with an A700 auto-

mated plate handling system (Stratedigm). For typical flow cytometry experiments, at least 3000 cells

were analyzed in each condition.

Flow cytometry data were analyzed using custom R scripts. Fluorescence channel values were nor-

malized to cell size by dividing by the cell side scatter. To analyze the protein titration experiments,

mScarlet-I fluorescence was used as a proxy for the level of the mScarlet-I fusion protein. Cells grown in

different DOX concentrations were pooled computationally and binned based on their mScarlet-I fluo-

rescence. For every combination of genotype and galactose concentration, 11 breaks between the first

and 99th percentile mCherry levels were defined in logarithmic space, resulting in ten equally spaced

64


<!-- Page 77 -->


bins. GAL signalling in each bin was summarized by averaging the fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)

channel fluorescence of all cells of a given replicate in logarithmic space. To account for bleed-through

of the mScarlet-I fluorescence into the FITC channel, the mean FITC fluorescence in 0 mM GAL was

subtracted in linear space. Replicate measurements were taken from separately grown cultures. For

plots with multiple summarized replicates, the mean and s.d. of background-subtracted bin means were

calculated in logarithmic space.

### 2.4.4 Galactose uptake rate measurement

Strains were pre-grown as described above, but the outgrowth culture was performed in a tube shaker

(230 rpm, 30 ◦C) with increased volume (5 mL). After three washes in synthetic minimal medium

without any carbon sources (see above), 1 mL of medium was inoculated to an inoculation OD600 of

0.02. After 0.5, 4 and 8 h, samples were taken by spinning down 150 µL of culture medium (3000 g,

3 min) and freezing the supernatant. Galactose concentrations in the culture supernatant were deter-

mined in duplicate using an enzymatic kit (l-Arabinose/d-Galactose Assay Kit, Megazyme). Conditions

where one of the time points had an s.d. above 0.5 or where less than 95% of the initial galactose was

taken up were excluded from further analysis. At every time point, 150 µL of culture was mixed with

50 µL of a 100-counting bead µL−1 suspension (CountBright, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and analyzed

using flow cytometry to obtain the cell concentrations and doubling time. To calculate the galactose

depletion rate (r), data were fitted to the following formula:

galext = galinit −N02t/tdr

where the external galactose concentrations (galext) at the given time points (t), the initial cell count

(N0) and the doubling time (td) were the fixed parameters, while the initial galactose concentration

(galinit) and the galactose depletion rate (r) were the free parameters. Mean fluorescence values in the

flow cytometry measurement at the final time point were used to quantify protein levels and GAL sig-

nalling in given DOX concentrations as described above.

### 2.4.5 Time-lapse microscopy

Strains were pre-grown and washed as described above. Cells were resuspended to an OD600 = 0.1 and

7.5 µL were used to inoculate a 1.5-ml culture of synthetic minimal medium with the appropriate car-

bon concentrations. After shaking for 7 h in a tube shaker (230 rpm, 30 ◦C), cells were pelleted (3000 g,

3 min) and resuspended in 20 µL medium. Concentrated cultures were loaded into concanavalin A-

coated channels in a flow cell (µ-Slide VI 0.1, Ibidi) and attached using centrifugation (100 g, 3 min).

To ensure constant carbon concentrations and to remove daughter cells, the medium was perfused

through the channels at a flow rate of 10 µL min−1. Cells were imaged every 15 min using fluorescence

microscopy with a charge-coupled device camera (Orca-R2, Hamamutsu), a ×60/1.40 objective (Plan

Apo VC ×60/1.40 Oil, Nikon), a motorized XY-stage (ProScan II, Prior), a metal-halide lamp system

(Lumen 200 Pro, Prior) and an emission filter wheel (Prior) on an Eclipse Ti inverted microscope

(Nikon). To quantify Ubi-Y-mNeonGreen fluorescence, cells were excited using a 500/24-nm filter;

fluorescence was collected with a 542/27-nm filter. To quantify mTagBFP2 fluorescence, cells were ex-

cited using a 390/40-nm filter; fluorescence was collected with a 452/45-nm filter. Image acquisition

was controlled using custom Python scripts. At least 250 cells were analyzed in each condition.

Images were segmented based on mTagBFP2 fluorescence using software available at https://

github.com/alexxijielu/yeast_segmentation. Custom Python scripts were used to track individual

cells. Briefly, segmented cells were assigned to a cell trace when they were the closest cell within 30 pix-

els (estimated by the distance between the centroids of the segmented objects), which was between

0.75× and 1.5× of the traced cell size (estimated by the area of the segmented objects) in the previ-

ous image. For each cell and image, the average pixel intensity of the Ubi-Y-mNeonGreen fluorescence

measurement was subtracted with a constant value (1675) to correct for background fluorescence.

## flux-dependent via non-canonical regulation

## of Mig1

## Ang Li & Michael Springer

In this chapter, we attempt to understand glucose sensing in the glucose repression pathway. We find

that glucose repression depends on glucose metabolic flux instead of glucose concentration. We exclude

the roles of all previously characterized glucose sensors in this process. The long-standing hypothesis of

hexokinase being the primary flux sensor for glucose repression is also ruled out. Finally, we find that

control of glucose repression by metabolic flux involves non-canonical regulation of Mig1 activity.
